title: Sort by Size, Then Ask an Antibody

scenes.tts: A cell extract holds thousands of different proteins. How can you follow just one? First, sort by size. This step is called S D S page. Heat the extract in S D S, a detergent. It unfolds each protein and coats it with negative charge, roughly in proportion to its length. Pull the mixture through a gel with an electric field. Small proteins travel farther than large ones.
scenes.visual: A crowd of proteins in an extract, one kind in yellow; SDS turns them into charged rods; they run down a gel and sort into bands by size.
scenes.narration: A cell extract holds thousands of different proteins. How can you follow just one? First, sort by size. This step is called SDS-PAGE. Heat the extract in SDS, a detergent. It unfolds each protein and coats it with negative charge, roughly in proportion to its length. Pull the mixture through a gel with an electric field. Small proteins travel farther than large ones.

scenes.tts: Next, find. This step is the western blot. Move the sorted proteins from the gel onto a membrane. Then soak the membrane in an antibody against your protein. A second antibody carries an enzyme that makes light or colour. It marks where the first one stuck. You see a band at one size.
scenes.visual: The gel's bands move to a membrane; a labelled antibody block docks on the yellow band, a second block with an enzyme docks on it; the band lights up alone.

scenes.tts: One antibody is raised against a short piece of a protein with a phosphate on one residue. It is chosen so that it binds only when the phosphate is present. A blot with it reads one site, from cells, minutes after a signal arrives. Blot the same samples with an antibody to the whole protein as well. Otherwise you cannot tell more phosphate from more protein.
scenes.visual: An antibody block docks on a phosphate badge but not on a protein without one; then two blots of the same samples, side by side (idealised example).

scenes.tts: An antibody has limits. It answers the question you built it for, so it cannot find a site nobody suspected. It reports that a band got darker, not what fraction of the molecules carry the phosphate. The antibody can bind the wrong protein. So a careful blot includes a sample in which the protein or the phosphate is missing. And a blot averages millions of cells.
scenes.visual: Four panels appear in turn: an unsuspected site, a darker band with unknown fraction, the wrong protein plus a control sample, many cells in one band.
